refsect2.title: Hierarchies of unit specification files
refsect2.para: It's possible to create subdirectories in @INSTALLCONFIGDIR@ and install unit specification files in the subdirectories. This has several important consequences.

listitem.para: In the unit specification file, the name field still matches the filename (without the subdirectory's name), but the unit's logical, or hierarchical, name includes its subdirectory. For example: @INSTALLCONFIGDIR@/networking/vpn unit's logical name is networking/vpn and it contains an identifying name: vpn.
vlad commands use hierarchical names. vlad start networking/vpn refers to the vpn unit specification file in the networking subdirectory.

Dependency names are "relative" to the unit's hierarchical name. For example: a networking/vpn unit that specifies Requires: interfaces refers to networking/interfaces. Its Enabled: ../system/networking defines that it's enabled in the system/networking runlevel (which can also be defined as Enabled: /system/networking).

refsect2.para: This happens to be how (for example) Enabled: system/graphical works in unit specification files that get installed, ordinarily, in @INSTALLCONFIGDIR@. It's just a relative pathname.

refsect2.title: Compound unit specification files
refsect2.para: It's possible to define multiple unit specification files in a single file, as multiple YAML documents. This is called a compound unit specification file. They are separated by a single line containing three dashes:

informalexample.programlisting:
name: networking description: bring up networking enabled: system/networking requires: - networking/interfaces - networking/vpn starting: type: oneshot stopping: type: target --- name: interfaces description: enable network interfaces starting: command: /usr/bin/networking start stopping: command: /usr/bin/networking stop --- name: vpn description: enable vpns starting: after: interfaces command: /usr/bin/vpn start stopping: before: interfaces command: /usr/bin/vpn stop
version: 1

refsect2.para: This hypothetical compound unit specification file is presumed to be installed in @INSTALLCONFIGDIR@/networking. Summary of the end results:

listitem.para: The name of the initial YAML section must, as usual, match its filename. This sets the hierarchical name of the unit specification file. Its logical name is also what it normally is (if this unit specification file gets installed in the local subdirectory, for example, its logical name becomes local/networking).

All remaining YAML sections in the compound file define additional units as if they were installed in a subdirectory named after the unit specification file. The above example creates hierarchical names networking/interfaces and networking/vpn, in addition to the main networking one.
All rules for specifying dependencies use unit specifications' hierarchical names.

version: 1 requirement still holds. It should still be the last key in the physical file. It now appears as part of the last YAML section, but its only purpose is to enforce specification file loading integrity. It has no other impact on any specification file's properties.

note.para: vlad enable, vlad disable and vlad mask can only be used with the unit specification file's "main" logical name, in this case networking. Except for the fact that they're defined in a single, compound file, networking, networking/interfaces and networking/vpn are independent units and, subject to all the usual rules; they can be started or stopped individually. However vlad mask networking logically masks all of them together (same for enabling and disabling where appropriate, see for more information).

The alternative approach of using subdirectories allows each individual unit in the subdirectory to be masked, enabled or disabled. On the other hand, using this example, it won't be possible to have a logical networking unit, because it matches a subdirectory name.
